properties.statement:
CORRECTION, SAME SESSION, BEFORE ANYTHING ACTED ON IT: I recorded a defect saying `export_graph` silently deletes property values and that the divergence guard cannot see properties. IT WAS WRONG, AND THE GUARD'S OWN MESSAGE WAS RIGHT. The offending node has been DELETED rather than retired, because it was never true — a mistake is deleted, history is retired (retire-from-design's one question). WHAT I OBSERVED, and it was real: a live export wrote `granularity`/`volatility` on 54 artifacts where the committed file carried 162, while the tool said 'nothing in it would be lost'. WHAT I THEN ASSUMED WITHOUT TESTING: that the missing 108 were VALUES, and therefore that a guard which failed to flag them was blind to property-level loss. THE PROBE THAT SETTLES IT, which cost one command: round-trip the SAME live graph through the repo's freshly-built binary with tools/export_via_binary.py and count again.
    live via 0.24.0 server          artifacts=162  with granularity= 54
    re-exported via 0.25.0 binary   artifacts=162  with granularity=162
    committed                       artifacts=162  with granularity=162
Identical to committed. NOTHING WAS LOST. 162 is EVERY artifact in the design, which was the clue sitting in plain sight: a property present on literally all of them is a DEFAULT being serialized, not intent somebody recorded. v0.25.0 writes schema defaults into the export and v0.24.0 does not, so the 108 are `atomic`/`stable` defaults and the 54 are the ones actually set by hand. THE REAL FINDING UNDERNEATH, and it is worth more than the false one: THIS IS THE MEASUREMENT BL-198 ASKED FOR. That item (`epoch:planned-one-write-surface`) says 'stop serializing defaults, but measure the cost to compare_designs and the merge driver FIRST'. Here is the cost, measured on live data: two builds one release apart produce 108 phantom property-level `changed` findings in compare_designs for a design nobody edited — enough noise to make an agent invent a data-loss defect and block a PR on it. Serialized defaults are not free, and the instrument that reports them cannot tell a default from a decision. A COMPARISON THAT CANNOT SAY WHICH SIDE MEANT IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS AN EDGE THAT CANNOT SAY WHO ASSERTED IT (DUPLICATES `basis`, which cost dev_storyflow ten proposed deletions) — the fix there was to make provenance explicit rather than to tune the detector, and the same argument applies. HOW THE ERROR HAPPENED, since that is the reusable part: `compare_designs` reported 108 property differences and I read a DIFFERENCE as a LOSS, then reasoned three steps forward from it — through 'the daemon holds the lock so no other process could have written' — to a confident mechanism, and wrote it into a PR body and a handoff note before running the one command that checks it. THE TOOL NEVER CLAIMED LOSS; I DID. This is the session's own theme turned on its author: a confident answer from something that never looked. The standing lesson holds in both directions — evaluate the tool independently, and evaluate your own reading of the tool just as hard.
